title: Yali's Question
book: Guns, Germs and Steel: A Short History of Everybody for the Last 13,000 Years
author: Jared Diamond
field: Big history, and how to judge a theory
wiifm: The last book of the collection goes deepest, why some peoples had empires to lose in the first place, and then we take it apart. Today is as much a lesson in how to judge a grand theory as it is a lesson in prehistory, and the four questions at the end are worth more than any single explanation in the book. You will also get the single best distinction in this whole week: proximate cause versus ultimate cause.

b: In July 1972, on a beach in New Guinea, an American biologist studying bird evolution fell into conversation with a local politician called Yali. Yali was charismatic, politically formidable and curious about where things came from. They talked about the arrival of Europeans, about what had changed, and then Yali asked a question.
Why was it, he wanted to know, that white people had developed so much cargo and brought it to New Guinea, while his own people had so little of their own?

Jared Diamond thought it the best question anyone had ever put to him, and partly because of what it was not. Yali was not asking why Europeans were cleverer. He had worked alongside Europeans for years and privately rated them about average. He was asking a material and historical question, and in 1972 the available answers in respectable circles were either embarrassed silence or something with race in it.
Twenty-five years later Diamond published his answer. It won the Pulitzer Prize in 1998, sold in enormous quantities, and has been argued about ever since.
ch.cap: On a New Guinea beach, Yali asks about the cargo

ch.h: The physiologist who kept going back
b: Diamond is an unusual person to have written a universal history, and the oddness of his route is part of why the book reads as it does.

Born in Boston in 1937, he trained in physiology and took a doctorate on membrane biophysics at Cambridge, then spent a long academic career at UCLA working on, among other things, the gall bladder. That is his profession: a laboratory scientist studying how fluids move across membranes.

His father, Louis Diamond, was a paediatrician who became a pioneer of research into childhood blood disease, and his mother was a teacher, a concert pianist and a linguist. He went to Harvard, then to Cambridge, then joined the medical school at UCLA in 1966. Much later he added a second professorship at the same university, in geography, which is the formal record of a career that had quietly changed direction. He first sketched the argument in a 1991 book, The Third Chimpanzee, before giving it a book of its own.

From 1964 he began making expeditions to New Guinea to study birds, and kept doing it for decades, surveying highland species, living in villages, learning what it takes to get calories out of a tropical forest. It was on one of those trips that he met Yali.

So the book is written by someone who came to history with a biologist's habits: look for the environmental variable, treat human populations as populations, and distrust explanations that rest on the properties of individuals. Those habits are the book's strength and the source of nearly every objection to it. He will not entertain a racial explanation, which in 1997 was a genuine public service. He is also inclined to find a geographical answer because that is the kind of answer his training equips him to see.
ch.cap: Diamond nets birds in the New Guinea highlands

b: He opens the case with an event. On 16 November 1532, in the highland town of Cajamarca, a Spanish force of 168 men under Francisco Pizarro, 62 on horses, 106 on foot, met Atahualpa, ruler of an empire of perhaps ten million people, who came to the square with an entourage of thousands and an army of around eighty thousand camped nearby.
Within hours the Spanish had captured Atahualpa and killed thousands of his people. They lost nobody.

Diamond then does the thing that makes the book worth reading even if you reject its thesis: he separates the layers of explanation. The proximate causes are steel swords and armour against quilted cotton, horses against infantry, firearms, and literacy, Pizarro knew how Cortés had taken Mexico, while Atahualpa knew nothing comparable about Spaniards. Also smallpox, which had already arrived ahead of the Spanish and killed Atahualpa's father, triggering the civil war that left the empire divided.

But none of that is an answer to Yali, because each proximate cause demands a further question. Why did the Spanish have steel, horses, writing and smallpox antibodies, and the Inca not? Proximate causes describe the mechanism of an outcome. Ultimate causes explain why the mechanism was available to one side.
ch.cap: Pizarro's 168 men face Atahualpa's army at Cajamarca

b: The first ultimate cause is agricultural raw material, and the argument is a lottery.

Of the world's large terrestrial herbivorous mammals, only a small handful, Diamond counts fourteen species, were ever domesticated, and the overwhelming majority of those were native to Eurasia. Domestication requires a specific and rare combination: the animal must breed in captivity, grow fast enough to be worth feeding, tolerate confinement and a social hierarchy with humans at the top, and not be inclined to kill you.

Africa has zebras, and zebras fail the test, they have a disposition to bite and not let go, and nobody has ever built a cavalry out of them. The Americas lost most of their candidate megafauna thousands of years earlier. The same lottery applies to plants: the Fertile Crescent happened to hold a cluster of high-protein, self-pollinating, easily stored grasses and pulses that could be farmed with little genetic modification.
The consequence is not just food. Draught animals mean ploughing and transport. Herds mean manure, wool, milk and, the point of the sixth chapter, pathogens.

Diamond argues that food production arose independently in perhaps nine places, from the Fertile Crescent and China to Mesoamerica, the Andes, the eastern United States and the highlands of New Guinea itself. The starter kits were wildly unequal. New Guinea's farmers had taro, bananas and sugar cane, crops low in protein, and no animal to pull a plough.
ch.cap: Cows and horses are tamed; the zebra will not be

b: Then the argument that produced the book's most memorable image. Eurasia's great axis runs east to west; the Americas and Africa run north to south.

A crop package domesticated in the Fertile Crescent could spread thousands of miles along a roughly constant latitude, similar day length, similar seasonality, similar rainfall and disease, reaching Ireland in one direction and the Indus in the other without needing to be reinvented. A crop moving north or south crosses climate zones every few hundred miles, and has to be re-adapted or dies.

So the same innovation travels further and compounds longer on an east-west continent. Combine the three elements and you have the machine: better domesticates produce surplus; surplus produces dense populations, stored food and people who do not farm, soldiers, scribes, metallurgists, administrators; the easy axis lets all of it propagate and recombine. Steel and writing are downstream.

Diamond's illustrations are vivid. The llama and the guinea pig, domesticated in the Andes, never reached Mexico, and the turkey of Mexico never reached the Andes, though the two regions were barely two thousand miles apart. The peoples of Mexico even invented the wheel, but used it only on what appear to be toys, because they had no animal to pull a cart.

The transferable insight sits here rather than in the prehistory. Diffusion beats invention. An advantage that can travel unchanged into the next market accumulates; one that must be rebuilt each time does not.
ch.cap: Crops race along Eurasia; north-south continents block them

b: The strongest chapter is about disease, and it is the part of the thesis that has best survived.

Crowd epidemic diseases need two things: dense human populations to sustain transmission, and a reservoir of herd animals from which pathogens can jump species. Eurasia had both for thousands of years, and paid for them with millennia of epidemics that killed enormous numbers and left the descendants of survivors with some inherited resistance.

The Americas had dense cities. They had almost no herd animals, and therefore bred very few comparable pathogens of their own. When the two populations met, the exchange was violently asymmetrical: smallpox, measles, influenza and typhus moving one way, with mortality estimates for the indigenous population of the Americas running as high as ninety per cent across the following century, against a far thinner traffic in the other direction.
The uncomfortable conclusion is that the decisive European weapon was not the gun. It was several thousand years of living in close proximity to cattle and pigs.
ch.cap: Germs from herd animals cross the ocean with the ships

ch.h: Writing was invented only a few times
b: Steel and germs get the title, but some of Diamond's best pages are on writing, the piece of equipment that let Pizarro know what Cortés had done. The striking fact is how rarely it was invented. On his account writing arose independently only a handful of times: certainly in Sumer before 3000 BC and in Mexico before 600 BC, probably in Egypt and China too. Everywhere else it was borrowed.

Borrowing came in two forms. Blueprint copying takes a working system and adapts it, the way alphabets descended from early Semitic scripts spread around the Mediterranean. Idea diffusion takes only the notion that speech can be written down and rebuilds the details from scratch. His favourite example is Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith in the American South who could not read English but had seen settlers making marks on paper, and who around 1820 devised a syllabary for the Cherokee language on his own. Within a few years much of the Cherokee nation could read and write it.

And writing only appeared where farming had produced the right kind of society: dense, stratified, with storehouses to account for and officials to do the accounting. The earliest Sumerian tablets are mostly lists of goods, livestock and rations. Writing began as bookkeeping.

There is a lesson here for anyone proud of their originality. Truly new inventions are rare and slow. Most progress is borrowing, either copying the blueprint or taking the idea and building it again, and the societies that pulled ahead were the ones best placed to borrow.
ch.cap: A Sumerian scribe presses grain and sheep into clay

b: Food production did one more thing, and it explains why Pizarro arrived with an empire behind him rather than a village. Diamond sorts human societies into four rough types by size: bands of a few dozen, tribes of a few hundred, chiefdoms of thousands, and states of tens of thousands and more. The ladder can only be climbed with surplus, because only surplus feeds people who do not grow food.

Once a society is so large that most people are strangers to one another, it needs a way to stop strangers fighting and a way to organise big works. The answer, again and again, was a ruling class that took a share of what everyone produced and handed some of it back. Diamond calls this, with a biologist's bluntness, kleptocracy. He lists the ways such rulers keep their position: disarming the population, redistributing some of the take in public works and favours, keeping order, and building an ideology or a religion that makes the whole arrangement feel right.

This matters for Yali's question because states, not bands, build ships, fund expeditions and smelt steel. Pizarro was the agent of a monarchy with tax revenue, bankers and printing presses. The people of New Guinea, in Diamond's telling, were not less capable. They lived in small farming societies spread across steep, divided valleys, where the conditions for empire never came together.
ch.cap: Farmers carry their surplus up to the ruler's walls

b: There is a hole in the theory and Diamond knows it. If Eurasian advantages are the explanation, the Eurasian power that should have taken the world was China.

China had agriculture earlier than Europe, more people, gunpowder, printing, the compass, paper, a sophisticated bureaucracy, and between 1405 and 1433 the largest navy on earth. Admiral Zheng He took seven enormous fleets into the Indian Ocean, reaching India, Arabia and the east coast of Africa. The ships were the largest wooden vessels ever built.
Then the court decided the voyages were a waste, and they stopped. The shipyards were allowed to decay, records were destroyed, and ocean-going fleets were effectively abandoned.

Diamond's answer is a geographical one about fragmentation. China's geography favours unification, a smooth coast, great navigable rivers running east, no serious internal barriers, so one decision governed everything. Europe's broken coastline, mountain ranges and peninsulas sustained dozens of competing states, so Columbus could be refused by Portugal and by Spanish advisers and still eventually get funded. Unity gave China scale and a single point of failure. Fragmentation gave Europe redundancy.

Diamond spells out Columbus's journey through the courts of Europe. An Italian by birth, he tried the king of Portugal, then the Spanish dukes of Medina-Sidonia and Medina-Celi, and was turned down again and again before Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain finally agreed in 1492. In a single empire, the first refusal would have been the last.
It is the most immediately useful chapter in the book, and the one most at risk of being a story fitted to its ending.
ch.cap: Zheng He's fleet rots while its voyage records burn

ch.h: The case against, and four questions
b: The most thorough attack came from the geographer James Blaut in 1999, and it cannot be dismissed as a defence of the old story, because Blaut was equally hostile to Eurocentrism.

On the famous east-west axis his objection is sharp: it is really a climate argument wearing a geometric costume, and Eurasia's temperate belt is in fact cut by the world's largest deserts and highest mountains, so it is nothing like as connected as the map implies, while north-south diffusion in Africa and the Americas did in fact occur. He also charges Diamond with selecting the comparisons that fit and with sliding into a determinism that cannot account for events after 1500.

The second line of attack comes from economics. Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson argue in Why Nations Fail that geography cannot explain the variation we actually care about, because the sharpest differences in prosperity occur between places with near-identical geography and different institutions, the two Koreas, the two halves of Nogales.

Diamond has answered that he is describing what environment made likely, not what it made inevitable, and in later books, Collapse in 2005 among them, he gave much more weight to the choices societies make. Critics reply that the tone of Guns, Germs and Steel promises more than that.

So here is the procedure, and it is the real souvenir of this week. One: what would falsify this? Two: is any step circular, is a cause being evidenced by its own effect? Three: at what scale does it actually work, and does it still work at the scale I care about? Four: who or what is being compressed out of it? Diamond's germs chapter passes all four comfortably. His axis argument struggles on the first and the second. Apply the same four questions to the next confident grand theory you are offered, including the ones you like.
ch.cap: Critics test the grand theory with four questions

take: Steel, horses, writing and smallpox explain how 168 Spaniards took Cajamarca; they do not explain why one side had them. Run both layers on your own last win or loss, proximate causes generate activity, ultimate causes are where the decisions are.
Raw materials are a lottery nobody earned

Only about fourteen large mammal species were ever domesticated and most were Eurasian; zebras fail the test on temperament alone. Before crediting anyone's brilliance, including your own, ask what was simply available to them.

Eurasia's east-west axis let one crop package travel from Ireland to the Indus at constant latitude, so advantages compounded instead of dying locally. Prefer the advantage that can move unchanged into the next market over the one that must be rebuilt each time.

Eurasia bred crowd diseases over millennia and carried partial resistance; the Americas had cities but almost no herd animals, and lost as much as ninety per cent of their population. The decisive weapon was proximity to cattle, not firearms.

One court decision ended the Chinese treasure fleets in the 1430s, while Columbus could be refused repeatedly and still get funded. Build two routes to a yes in your own business, so that a single no, including yours on a bad day, cannot kill a good idea.
Unity buys scale and a single point of failure

China's geography favoured one decision governing everything; Europe's broken coastline sustained competing states and therefore redundancy. Ask of any consolidation what it is centralising and what it is removing as a backup.
Check whether a theory is a climate argument in costume

Blaut's objection to the axis is that it restates climate geometrically while ignoring the deserts and mountains cutting Eurasia. A memorable image is not evidence, and the more quotable a mechanism is, the harder you should test it.
Carry the four questions, not the conclusions

What would falsify this? Is any step circular? At what scale does it hold? Who is compressed out of it? Diamond's germs chapter passes all four; his axis argument struggles on two. Use them on the next grand theory you are offered, especially one you want to believe.
recall: What exactly did Yali ask, and why did Diamond think it the right question?

On a New Guinea beach in July 1972 Yali asked why white people had developed so much cargo and brought it to New Guinea while his own people had so little of their own. Diamond valued it because it was framed materially and historically rather than as a question about intelligence, Yali had worked with Europeans and rated them about average.
Distinguish the proximate from the ultimate causes of Cajamarca.

Proximate: steel swords and armour, horses, firearms, and literacy, Pizarro knew how Cortés had taken Mexico while Atahualpa knew nothing comparable, plus smallpox, which had already killed Atahualpa's father and triggered a civil war. Ultimate: why one side possessed steel, horses, writing and inherited disease resistance at all, which is the question about domesticable species, continental axes and livestock-borne pathogens.
State the axis argument and Blaut's objection.

Eurasia's main axis runs east to west, so crops and animals could spread thousands of miles at roughly constant latitude, day length and climate, letting advantages accumulate; the Americas and Africa run north to south, slicing diffusion across climate zones. Blaut answers that this is a climate argument in geometric costume: Eurasia's temperate belt is cut by the largest deserts and highest mountains on earth, and north-south diffusion demonstrably did occur.
What does Diamond mean by idea diffusion, and who is his favourite example?

Idea diffusion is borrowing only the concept of an invention and rebuilding the details, as opposed to copying a working blueprint. His example is Sequoyah, who could not read English but, knowing that settlers wrote, created a Cherokee syllabary around 1820 that much of his nation soon learned.
Why does Diamond call early states kleptocracies, and how do they hold power?

Large societies of strangers need rulers who keep order and organise big works, and those rulers take a share of everyone's produce and keep much of it. They hold power by disarming the population, redistributing some of the take, keeping the peace and building an ideology or religion that justifies the arrangement.
note: Documented: Diamond's birth in 1937, his parents' careers, his training in physiology and membrane biophysics, his New Guinea bird expeditions from 1964, the July 1972 conversation with Yali as he recounts it in the book's prologue, The Third Chimpanzee of 1991 and the 1998 Pulitzer. The Cajamarca figures, the count of fourteen domesticated large mammals, the roughly nine centres of food production, the dates for independent writing, Sequoyah and the kleptocracy framework are Diamond's. Indigenous mortality estimates vary widely between scholars; the ninety per cent figure is at the high end of the range. Principal critics cited: James Blaut (1999), and Acemoglu and Robinson.
words: Nearest in a chain of causes, the immediate mechanism rather than the deeper reason behind it.
Steel, horses and guns were the proximate causes of the Spanish victory at Cajamarca; Diamond's book is a hunt for the ultimate ones.
Rule by those who take a share of everyone else's wealth for themselves.
Diamond bluntly calls the ruling classes of early states kleptocracies, which kept their place by disarming people and handing back some of the take.
A writing system in which each symbol stands for a whole syllable rather than a single sound.
Sequoyah, who could not read English, invented a syllabary for the Cherokee language around 1820.
The large animals of a region or period, usually meaning those weighing more than a person.
The Americas lost most of their large-mammal megafauna thousands of years ago, leaving almost nothing to domesticate.
Capable of being proved wrong by some possible evidence, which is what makes a claim testable.
The first of the four questions for any grand theory, Diamond's included, is whether it is falsifiable at all.

biz: One court decision ended China's treasure fleets, while Columbus was turned down again and again and still found a backer, because Europe had many courts. For a broker, the equivalent is a lender panel where one lender's no does not end a suitable application. This week, check how many enquiries last quarter were declined by your first-choice lender and then placed elsewhere, and how many had nowhere else to go. If the second number is large, widen the panel. The aim is never to push every customer into a loan, but to make sure a suitable case is not lost to one lender's appetite on one day.
The ultimate cause of a lost client

When a Debt Support Direct client goes quiet, the proximate cause on the file is usually simple: no answer to calls. Diamond would ask the ultimate question. Was it shame, fear of opening post, a letter full of jargon, or a contact method that did not suit someone in crisis? This week, take the last twenty clients who disengaged and write two columns for each: what happened, and what made it possible. Then change the cause, not the chasing: plain-language messages, a WhatsApp option, one named adviser. More calls is the wrong lesson, and with vulnerable clients it can do real harm.
connects: Harari and Diamond both treat the coming of farming as the hinge that produced surplus, cities, rulers and writing, and both ask whether it made ordinary lives better.
Taleb's narrative fallacy, a neat story fitted to an outcome after the fact, is the risk Diamond runs in explaining why China stopped exploring and Europe did not.
Tetlock's insistence on asking what would prove a forecast wrong is the first of the four questions this book leaves you for testing any grand theory.
recap:
In July nineteen seventy-two, on a beach in New Guinea, a local politician called Yali asked an American biologist a question. Why did white people have so much cargo, and his own people so little? He was not asking who was cleverer. He had worked with Europeans and rated them about average. He was asking what had happened.

The biologist was Jared Diamond, a Boston-born physiologist who studied how fluids cross membranes and, from nineteen sixty-four, spent decades in New Guinea studying birds. Twenty-five years after that conversation he published his answer, Guns, Germs and Steel, and it won the Pulitzer Prize.

He opens at Cajamarca in fifteen thirty-two, where a hundred and sixty-eight Spaniards captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa in front of thousands of his people, and lost nobody. Then he hands you the best tool in the book, the difference between proximate and ultimate causes. Steel, horses, guns and writing explain how it happened. They do not explain why the Spanish had them and the Inca did not.

His first answer is a lottery of plants and animals. Only about fourteen large mammals were ever domesticated, and most of them lived in Eurasia. Zebras bite and will not let go, and nobody has ever built a cavalry out of them.

His second is the shape of the continents. Eurasia runs east to west, so crops could spread along the same latitude from Ireland to the Indus. The Americas and Africa run north to south, through one climate after another. An advantage that can travel unchanged keeps on compounding.

His third, and the strongest, is germs. Thousands of years of living beside cattle and pigs gave Eurasians terrible diseases and some resistance to them. The peoples of the Americas had almost no herd animals, and when the two worlds met, smallpox did more than any sword.

His fourth is about fragmentation. China had the largest fleet on earth in the early fifteenth century, and one court decision ended it. Columbus was turned down again and again, but Europe had many courts, and in the end one of them said yes.

Then come the critics. The geographer James Blaut said the east to west axis is a climate argument in disguise. Economists point to the two Koreas, with the same geography and very different fortunes. So test any grand theory with four questions. What would prove it wrong? Is any step circular? At what scale does it really work? And who has been left out of it?

The line to remember is this. Before you credit anyone's genius, ask what was simply within their reach.
